title: Die gar traurige Geschichte mit dem Feuerzeug
titleEn: The Very Sad Story of the Matches
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: The darkest of Heinrich Hoffmann’s 1845 cautionary verses: Paulinchen, left alone in the house, plays with the fire-making things and burns to ashes, while the two cats warn her, wail, and at last sit down and weep. The warning was a real one — open flames everywhere and children in long cotton frocks — and Hoffmann grants no reprieve: what is left is a little heap of ash and a pair of shoes. »Feuerzeug« in 1845 is not a cigarette lighter but the household kit for striking a light, and the »Hölzchen« Paulinchen lights is a match.

sentences.t:
Paulinchen war allein zu Haus,
die Eltern waren beide aus.
sentences.l:
Little-Pauline was alone at home,
the parents were both out.
sentences.i:
Little Pauline was alone at home;
her parents were both out.
sentences.n: »Paulinchen« is the -chen diminutive again, this time on a name: little Pauline. »aus sein« = ‘to be out (of the house)’ — the »aus« is the whole predicate. And German says »die Eltern«, ‘the parents,’ where English wants ‘her parents’: the possessor is taken as obvious, the same habit as with body parts.

sentences.t:
Als sie nun durch das Zimmer sprang
mit leichtem Mut und Sing und Sang,
da sah sie plötzlich vor sich stehn
ein Feuerzeug, nett anzusehn.
sentences.l:
As she now through the room leapt
with light spirit and sing and song,
there saw she suddenly before herself stand
a match-box, nice to look at.
sentences.i:
As she went skipping through the room,
light-hearted and singing away,
all at once she saw standing before her
a box of matches, pretty to look at.
sentences.n: »das Feuerzeug« is literally ‘fire-gear’ — the household means of making fire; in 1845 that means the box of friction matches (»Hölzchen«, little sticks) that had only lately come in, not a lighter and no longer flint and steel. »Mut« here is not ‘courage’ but ‘spirits, mood’: »mit leichtem Mut« = light-hearted. »Sing und Sang« is a fixed jingling pair, roughly ‘singing and humming.’ »sah sie … stehn« — »sehen« takes a bare infinitive, as English does: ‘saw it stand.’ »anzusehn« is the separable »ansehen« with the »zu« tucked inside it: an-zu-sehn, ‘to look at.’

sentences.t:
»Ei,« sprach sie, »ei, wie schön und fein!
Das muß ein trefflich Spielzeug sein.
sentences.l:
“Ah,” spoke she, “ah, how lovely and fine!
That must a splendid plaything be.
sentences.i:
“Oh,” said she, “oh, how lovely and fine!
That must be a splendid toy.
sentences.n: »Ei!« is a little cry of pleased surprise. »trefflich« = ‘excellent, splendid’ — elevated and old-fashioned; and it stands uninflected before the noun (»ein trefflich Spielzeug« rather than »ein treffliches Spielzeug«), an older poetic licence that verse keeps alive. »Spielzeug« answers »Feuerzeug« a line above — the same »-zeug« ending, and the whole disaster in one rhyme. »sprach« as before, the storybook past.

sentences.t:
Ich zünde mir ein Hölzchen an,
wie's oft die Mutter hat getan.«
sentences.l:
I light for-myself a little-stick up,
as it often the mother has done.”
sentences.i:
I shall light myself a little match,
as Mother has often done.”
sentences.n: »anzünden« is separable, and the »an« is stranded at the line’s end — the tailor’s »ab« trick, gentler. »mir« is the dative of interest, ‘for myself,’ which English can just about keep here. »ein Hölzchen« is literally ‘a little piece of wood’: what a match was called. »wie’s« = »wie es«. The present »zünde« carries a future sense, as German freely does.

sentences.t:
Und Minz und Maunz, die Katzen,
erheben ihre Tatzen.
sentences.l:
And Minz and Maunz, the cats,
raise their paws.
sentences.n: The cats’ names are cat-noises. »maunzen« is a real verb — ‘to yowl, to whine’ — and »Minz« has no verb behind it, only the chime with it. They are left as they stand. »die Tatze« is the paw of a clawed beast; two lines on, the same paws are ordinary »Pfoten«.

sentences.t:
Sie drohen mit den Pfoten:
»Der Vater hat's verboten!
sentences.l:
They threaten with the paws:
“The father has it forbidden!
sentences.i:
They threaten with their paws:
“Father has forbidden it!
sentences.n: »hat’s« = »hat es«. »verbieten« (‘to forbid’) is one of the verbs whose past participle takes no ge-: »verboten«. »der Vater« with the article is how a household spoke of him — ‘Father.’ The cats invoke an authority that is not in the room; that is the whole of their power.

sentences.t:
Miau! Mio! Miau! Mio!
laß stehn! sonst brennst du lichterloh!«
sentences.l:
Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
let it stand! else burn you blazing-bright!”
sentences.i:
Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
Leave it be, or you will go up in flames!”
sentences.n: »etwas stehen lassen« = ‘to leave a thing alone, leave it where it stands’; the object is simply understood. »sonst« = ‘or else,’ the tailor’s word. »lichterloh« is ‘in full blaze’ — from »loh«, an old word for flame; it survives in modern German only in this one phrase, »lichterloh brennen«.

sentences.t:
Paulinchen hört die Katzen nicht!
Das Hölzchen brennt gar hell und licht,
sentences.l:
Little-Pauline hears the cats not!
The little-stick burns quite bright and light,
sentences.i:
Little Pauline does not listen to the cats!
The little match burns bright and clear,
sentences.n: »hören« with a plain accusative can mean ‘heed, listen to’ as well as ‘hear’ — she hears them perfectly well. »gar« = ‘quite, altogether’ (the same »gar« as in the title, »die gar traurige Geschichte«). »hell und licht« doubles two words that both mean ‘bright’, for the sound of it.

sentences.t:
das flackert lustig, knistert laut,
grad wie ihr's auf dem Bilde schaut.
sentences.l:
it flickers merrily, crackles loudly,
just as you it on the picture behold.
sentences.i:
it flickers merrily and crackles loudly,
just as you see it in the picture.
sentences.n: »das« opening the line is the demonstrative pronoun taking up »das Hölzchen« — ‘that thing,’ ‘it.’ »grad« = »gerade«, clipped. »ihr« is the plural ‘you’: the narrator turns from the story to the children holding the book and points at the illustration, which is part of the telling and not an ornament. »auf dem Bilde« keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t:
Paulinchen aber freut sich sehr
und sprang im Zimmer hin und her.
sentences.l:
Little-Pauline however rejoices herself much
and leapt in-the room to and fro.
sentences.i:
But Pauline is delighted,
and went skipping about the room.
sentences.n: »aber« in second position = ‘but’: German may put it after the first element instead of at the head. »sich freuen« = ‘to be glad, delighted.’ »sehr« here is the ordinary modern intensifier, ‘very much’ — not the old ‘sorely’ it carried when Konrad screamed. And the tense jumps from present »freut« to past »sprang« inside one sentence, as verse does throughout this book.

sentences.t:
Doch Minz und Maunz, die Katzen,
erheben ihre Tatzen.
sentences.l:
But Minz and Maunz, the cats,
raise their paws.
sentences.n: The refrain returns with a single word changed: »Und« has become »Doch«, ‘but.’ Each return of these two lines shifts one word, and the shifts are the story’s clock.

sentences.t:
Sie drohen mit den Pfoten:
»Die Mutter hat's verboten!
sentences.l:
They threaten with the paws:
“The mother has it forbidden!
sentences.i:
They threaten with their paws:
“Mother has forbidden it!
sentences.n: Father last time, Mother this time: the refrain works through the household’s authorities one at a time, and neither of them is in the room.

sentences.t:
Miau! Mio! Miau! Mio!
wirf's weg! sonst brennst du lichterloh!«
sentences.l:
Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
throw it away! else burn you blazing-bright!”
sentences.i:
Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
Throw it away, or you will go up in flames!”
sentences.n: »wegwerfen« is separable: »wirf’s weg« = ‘throw it away.’ »wirf« is the du-imperative of »werfen«, which changes its vowel e → i in the imperative and in the du/er forms. The warning has moved from ‘leave it alone’ to ‘get rid of it’: too late either way.

sentences.t:
Doch weh! die Flamme faßt das Kleid,
die Schürze brennt, es leuchtet weit.
sentences.l:
But woe! the flame seizes the dress,
the apron burns, it shines far.
sentences.i:
But alas! the flame catches her dress,
the apron is alight, the glow carries far.
sentences.n: »fassen« = ‘to seize, take hold of’ — the flame grabs the dress rather than merely reaching it. »das Kleid« and »die Schürze«: the frock and the pinafore worn over it, what a child wore every day in the 1840s, and both of them cotton. »es leuchtet weit« is impersonal — the »es« names nothing; the light simply travels.

sentences.t:
Es brennt die Hand, es brennt das Haar,
es brennt das ganze Kind sogar.
sentences.l:
There burns the hand, there burns the hair,
there burns the whole child even.
sentences.i:
Her hand is burning, her hair is burning,
the whole child is burning, even.
sentences.n: »es brennt die Hand« is »die Hand brennt« with a placeholder »es« holding the front slot, so the verb can stand second and the real subject arrive after it. Three hammer-blows of the same construction, each subject larger than the last, until the third takes the child entire. »sogar« = ‘even.’

sentences.t:
Und Minz und Maunz, die schreien
gar jämmerlich zu zweien:
sentences.l:
And Minz and Maunz, they scream
quite piteously, two together:
sentences.i:
And Minz and Maunz — they cry out
most piteously, the two of them:
sentences.n: »die« is the demonstrative pronoun again, resuming the two cats: ‘they.’ »zu zweien« is an old dative-plural phrase, ‘the pair of them together.’ »jämmerlich« is built on »Jammer« (misery): ‘wretchedly, pitiably.’ Note what the refrain has done — this time the paws are not raised.

sentences.t:
»Herbei! Herbei! Wer hilft geschwind?
In Feuer steht das ganze Kind!
sentences.l:
“Hither! Hither! Who helps swiftly?
In fire stands the whole child!
sentences.i:
“Come here! Come here! Who will help, and quickly?
The whole child is standing in fire!
sentences.n: »herbei!« is a bare directional adverb used as a shout — ‘over here, to us!’ (the »her-« is always motion toward the speaker, as in »herzu« and »herein«). »geschwind« = ‘swiftly’, old-fashioned now. »In Feuer steht das ganze Kind« says the thing as flatly as it can be said, and that is where the horror is.

sentences.t:
Miau! Mio! Miau! Mio!
zu Hilf! das Kind brennt lichterloh!«
sentences.l:
Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
to help! the child burns blazing-bright!”
sentences.i:
Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
Help, help! the child is all in flames!”
sentences.n: »zu Hilf!« is »zu Hilfe!« clipped — the standing cry for help. And »lichterloh« a third time: the warning has come true in its own words.

sentences.t:
Verbrannt ist alles ganz und gar,
das arme Kind mit Haut und Haar;
sentences.l:
Burnt is everything wholly and entirely,
the poor child with skin and hair;
sentences.i:
Everything is burnt clean away,
the poor child, skin and hair and all;
sentences.n: The participle is fronted (»Verbrannt ist alles«) so that the outcome stands before anything else. »ganz und gar« = ‘utterly.’ »mit Haut und Haar« is a fixed phrase for total consumption — used of what a beast eats, and Hoffmann means it exactly.

sentences.t:
ein Häuflein Asche bleibt allein
und beide Schuh, so hübsch und fein.
sentences.l:
a little-heap of-ash remains alone
and both shoes, so pretty and fine.
sentences.i:
a little heap of ashes is all that is left,
and her two shoes, so pretty and fine.
sentences.n: »das Häuflein« — the -lein diminutive, the bookish counterpart of -chen. »allein« here is ‘only that, nothing else.’ »Schuh« is »Schuhe« clipped. And the last line gives the shoes the words Paulinchen gave the matches, »so hübsch und fein« against her own »wie schön und fein«: the pretty things outlast her.

sentences.t:
Und Minz und Maunz, die kleinen,
die sitzen da und weinen:
sentences.l:
And Minz and Maunz, the little ones,
they sit there and weep:
sentences.i:
And Minz and Maunz, the little ones —
there they sit and weep:
sentences.n: »die kleinen« is an adjective standing as a noun, ‘the little ones’; then »die« resumes them as a pronoun. The cats have shrunk: first they raised paws, then they screamed, now they are simply small.

sentences.t:
»Miau! Mio! Miau! Mio!
wo sind die armen Eltern! wo?«
sentences.l:
“Miaow! Mio! Miaow! Mio!
where are the poor parents! where?”
sentences.n: The exclamation mark where English expects a question mark is Hoffmann’s, and it turns the line from a question into a wail. Note who is pitied: »die armen Eltern« — the ones who must come home to this.

sentences.t:
Und ihre Tränen fließen
wie's Bächlein auf den Wiesen.
sentences.l:
And their tears flow
like the little-brook on the meadows.
sentences.i:
And their tears run down
like a little brook across the meadows.
sentences.n: »wie’s« is »wie das« here, though two stanzas ago the same apostrophe swallowed »es« — the elision takes whatever the meter can spare. »Bächlein«, another -lein diminutive. The story ends with no moral at all, only a picture: two cats crying a stream.
